text:
PSY 771 · ANOVA and Experimental Design
    R Scripts
    R code files for all topics covered in the course. New scripts will be added each week.
  




  Course Scripts
  Getting Started
  Work through these two scripts before the first class session.

  
    Script 1

    
      Introduction to R
      What R is, how to install it, and the core building blocks — arithmetic, objects, vectors, matrices, and data frames. Start here if you are new to R.
    

  

  
    Script 2

    
      Descriptives, Correlation & Regression
      A complete data analysis workflow: importing a real psychology dataset, computing descriptive statistics with psych::describe(), testing correlations with cor.test(), and fitting a multiple regression with lm().
    

  

  
    Script 3

    
      Z-Scores, Confidence Intervals, and the Z-Test
      Standardizing scores with the z-score formula and scale(), finding areas under the normal curve with pnorm(), constructing 80/90/95/99% confidence intervals with qnorm(), and writing a custom z.test() function in R.
    

  

  
    Weekly Scripts

    
      Coming soon
      Scripts for t-tests, one-way ANOVA, factorial ANOVA, repeated measures ANOVA, and mixed ANOVA will be posted here as we progress through the course.

title: Introduction to R
text:
What is R?
R is a free, open-source programming language and computing environment built for statistics and data analysis. It is widely used across psychology, education, public health, and the social sciences — and it is what we will use throughout this course.
Unlike point-and-click software such as SPSS, R is a scripting language. You write a sequence of instructions, and R executes them in order. This takes practice at first, but the payoff is significant: your analyses are reproducible, shareable, and easy to modify.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Why R?

Free and open source. R costs nothing and runs on Mac, Windows, and Linux.
Reproducible. Your entire analysis lives in a script you can re-run, share, or modify.
Publication quality. R produces clean, customizable figures ready for journals and presentations.
Community. Thousands of user-contributed packages extend R’s capabilities. Whatever analysis you need, there is almost certainly a package for it.
Industry and academia. R is used in research labs, tech companies, public health agencies, and psychology departments worldwide. Learning it now is a career-long investment.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Downloading R and RStudio
You need two things: R (the language) and RStudio (the editor that makes R easier to use). Think of R as the engine and RStudio as the dashboard.

Download R from cran.r-project.org

Choose your operating system (Mac or Windows)
Install the most recent version

Download RStudio Desktop (free) from posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop

Install after R is installed
Always open RStudio, not R directly


When RStudio opens you will see four panes:







Pane
What it does




Source (top-left)
Where you write and save scripts


Console (bottom-left)
Where R runs code and shows output


Environment (top-right)
Lists objects currently in memory


Files / Plots / Help (bottom-right)
Browse files, see plots, read documentation

title: Introduction to R
text:
R as a Calculator
The simplest thing R can do is arithmetic. Type any expression and press Enter:
1 + 1
[1] 2
The [1] at the start of every output line just means “first element of the result.” You will see it everywhere.
10 - 3        # subtraction
4 * 5         # multiplication
20 / 4        # division
2 ^ 8         # exponentiation  →  256
sqrt(144)     # square root     →  12
abs(-7)       # absolute value  →  7






TipThe # symbol marks a comment



Everything after # on a line is a comment — R ignores it when running the code. Use comments freely to explain what each line does. Your future self will thank you.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Objects
In R, you can store any value in a named object using the assignment arrow <-:
X <- 8
Now X holds the value 8. Call it by name to see it:
X
[1] 8
You can use objects in calculations just like raw numbers:
X + 2       # 10
X * X       # 64
sqrt(X)     # 2.828427
Object names are case-sensitive: X and x are two different objects.

Vectors
A vector is a sequence of values stored together. Create one with c() — short for “combine”:
Y <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
Y
[1] 1 2 3 4 5
Operations on a vector apply to every element at once:
Y + 10       # [1] 11 12 13 14 15
Y * 2        # [1]  2  4  6  8 10
Vectors can also hold text (called character strings):
names <- c("Alice", "Bob", "Carol")
names
[1] "Alice" "Bob"   "Carol"


Matrices
A matrix is a two-dimensional table of values — rows and columns. Create one with matrix():
Z <- matrix(1:9, nrow = 3, ncol = 3)
Z
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    4    7
[2,]    2    5    8
[3,]    3    6    9
Values fill in column by column by default. You can transpose with t(Z).

title: Introduction to R
text:
Data Frames and Classes
Real data is usually stored in a data frame — a table with rows (observations) and columns (variables). R comes with several built-in datasets for practice.
mtcars is a classic: 32 cars, 11 variables including miles per gallon, cylinders, horsepower, and weight.
head(mtcars)      # first 6 rows
Access a single column with $:
mtcars$cyl        # the cylinder variable
 [1] 6 6 4 6 8 6 8 4 4 6 6 8 8 8 8 8 8 4 4 4 4 8 8 8 8 4 4 4 8 6 8 4

Checking Classes
Every object in R has a class — a label that tells R (and you) what type of thing it is:
class(mtcars)        # "data.frame"
class(mtcars$cyl)    # "numeric"
class("hello")       # "character"
class(TRUE)          # "logical"
The class determines which functions can be applied. Most errors in R trace back to a class mismatch — feeding a character vector to a function that expects numbers, for example.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Descriptive Statistics
Once data is loaded, computing summary statistics is straightforward. The attach() function lets you refer to a dataset’s columns by name without the $:
attach(mtcars)

mean(mpg)     # mean
sd(mpg)       # standard deviation
var(mpg)      # variance
max(mpg)      # maximum
min(mpg)      # minimum
range(mpg)    # minimum and maximum together






WarningUse attach() carefully



attach() makes column names available globally, which is convenient but can cause confusion if two datasets share column names. For complex scripts, prefer dataset$variable notation or use the with() function.



Correlations
cor(mpg, hp)           # correlation between mpg and horsepower
cor(mtcars)            # full correlation matrix for all variables


summary() — your best friend
summary() gives you a five-number summary plus the mean for every numeric column:
summary(mtcars)
      mpg             cyl             disp             hp
 Min.   :10.40   Min.   :4.000   Min.   : 71.1   Min.   : 52.0
 1st Qu.:15.43   1st Qu.:4.000   1st Qu.:120.8   1st Qu.: 96.5
 Median :19.20   Median :6.000   Median :196.3   Median :123.0
 Mean   :20.09   Mean   :6.188   Mean   :230.7   Mean   :146.7
 3rd Qu.:22.80   3rd Qu.:8.000   3rd Qu.:326.0   3rd Qu.:180.0
 Max.   :33.90   Max.   :8.000   Max.   :472.0   Max.   :335.0

title: Introduction to R
text:
Basic Plots
R produces publication-quality graphics. The base graphics functions are quick to use and good for exploration.

Histogram
Visualize the distribution of a single variable:
hist(mpg,
     main  = "Distribution of Miles per Gallon",
     xlab  = "MPG",
     col   = "steelblue",
     border = "white")
Key arguments:



Argument
What it does




main
Plot title


xlab
x-axis label


col
Bar fill color


breaks
Number of bins (optional)





Boxplot
Visualize the distribution of a variable across groups:
boxplot(mpg ~ cyl,
        data = mtcars,
        main = "MPG by Number of Cylinders",
        xlab = "Cylinders",
        ylab = "Miles per Gallon",
        col  = c("steelblue", "tomato", "seagreen"))
The ~ (tilde) reads as “by” — MPG by cylinders.


Scatterplot
Visualize the relationship between two numeric variables:
plot(hp, mpg,
     main = "Horsepower vs. MPG",
     xlab = "Horsepower",
     ylab = "Miles per Gallon",
     pch  = 19,
     col  = "steelblue")
pch = 19 gives you solid circles. Try values 1–25 to see different point shapes.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Getting Help
When you are unsure how a function works, prefix it with ?:
?mean
?sqrt
?matrix
The Help pane opens with the function’s documentation: description, arguments, and worked examples. ??keyword searches all installed documentation.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Next Steps
You now have the foundations: objects, data frames, classes, descriptive statistics, and basic plots. The rest of the course builds on these — each week’s R script will introduce the functions needed for the statistical model we cover that week.
Continue with the PSY 371 R Basics page for additional exercises including importing data from CSV and working with real datasets.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Why Use R?

Free. R costs nothing and runs on Mac, Windows, and Linux.
Reproducible. Your entire analysis lives in a script you can re-run, share, or hand to a reviewer.
Powerful and flexible. From t-tests to multilevel models to machine learning — R handles it all.
Standard in research. R is the dominant tool in academic psychology and education research. Learning it now is an investment you will use throughout your career.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Installing R and RStudio
You need two things. Install them in order.

1. R — the language itself

Download from cran.r-project.org. Choose your operating system and install the current release.

2. RStudio — the editor that makes R easier to use

Download the free RStudio Desktop from posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop. Always open RStudio, not R directly.


Think of R as the engine and RStudio as the dashboard.

The RStudio Interface
When RStudio opens you will see four panes:







Pane
Purpose




Source (top-left)
Write and save your scripts here


Console (bottom-left)
Where R runs code and shows output


Environment (top-right)
Objects currently stored in memory


Files / Plots / Help (bottom-right)
Browse files, view plots, read documentation



Write your code in the Source pane and run it with Ctrl+Enter (Windows) or Cmd+Return (Mac). Results appear in the Console.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Classes
Every object in R has a class — a label that tells R what kind of thing it is and which operations are valid. You can check it with class():
class(8)            # "numeric"
class("hello")      # "character"
class(TRUE)         # "logical"
class(c(1,2,3))     # "numeric"






NoteWhy classes matter



Almost every error in R comes down to a class mismatch — trying to do math on a character vector, or passing a data frame to a function that expects a single number. Checking the class of your objects is the first debugging step.

title: Introduction to R
text:
A First Look at Data
Real datasets in R are stored as data frames — tables with rows (observations) and columns (variables). R ships with several built-in datasets for practice.
mtcars has data on 32 cars:
head(mtcars)       # first 6 rows
Use $ to pull out a single column by name:
mtcars$cyl         # cylinder counts for all 32 cars
 [1] 6 6 4 6 8 6 8 4 4 6 6 8 8 8 8 8 8 4 4 4 4 8 8 8 8 4 4 4 8 6 8 4
A few useful inspection functions:
dim(mtcars)        # rows, columns:  32  11
names(mtcars)      # variable names
class(mtcars)      # "data.frame"
class(mtcars$mpg)  # "numeric"
